dossier.public_summary: The dip is only seen as shallow and changes depth between sectors and even between transits, which a planet should not do. With no clear on-target centroid and a nearby star that could produce it, a blended or variable eclipse best explains the signal, not a 2.7-Earth-radius planet.

reasons.why: Depth varies significantly even within the same light-curve product (SPOC 2-min) and between sectors (per-sector p_constant=0.0005048, depth_change_pct=59.98). A planet on the target should give a consistent depth; changes within a source point to dilution/variability or a blend.
reasons.value: verdict=changes_within_a_source, p_constant_all=0.0004983530942001915, SPOC 2-min depth 1607 ppm to 975 ppm (p_constant=0.0006886096148826367)

reasons.why: Individual transits are inconsistent at >0.0003 significance, so the signal is not repeatable with the same depth even on the same star aperture. For a low-count signal this favors a few bad events or a blend over a planet.

Difference imaging gives no on-target confirmation and there is at least one star within one TESS pixel (21 arcsec) that can explain the 1128 ppm dip with a 13% eclipse. Combined with variable depth, a blended eclipsing binary / spot-driven dip is the best explanation. xgboost.planet_rank=0.05 supports this.
